projectDetails.name: AakashNet A Region-optimized, Low-cost, Hybrid Satellite-mesh Broadband System Designed For Indian Infrastructure And Socio-economic Constraints.
projectDetails.summary:
AakashNet is an indigenous Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite network designed to provide secure, high-speed, and affordable internet connectivity across India’s diverse terrain. We developed a phased-array based user terminal capable of dynamic beam steering through Ku/Ka band communication, linking directly with AakashNet satellites in orbit. These satellites form a laser-linked mesh network, enabling continuous data relay with minimal latency and reduced ground dependency.

The system directly addresses India’s connectivity challenges—bridging the digital divide in rural regions, providing encrypted communication for defense posts, and delivering in-flight and maritime internet without relying on foreign networks. With hardware locally produced by Indian agencies like ISRO, HAL, and BHEL, AakashNet ensures technological sovereignty and strategic independence.

By combining indigenous satellite manufacturing, reusable ISRO launches, and adaptive phased-array ground technology, AakashNet transforms connectivity into a national infrastructure asset—empowering governance, education, defense, and the digital economy.
projectDetails.details:
AakashNet is an indigenous Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-based broadband communication system designed to deliver secure, high-speed, and reliable connectivity across India’s diverse landscapes — from rural villages to defense borders, ships, and aircraft. It solves India’s connectivity gap by replacing dependency on terrestrial infrastructure like fiber and towers with a network of locally manufactured satellites and smart phased-array user terminals.

How It Works:
Each user terminal — the Aakash Jodak dish — houses around 1280 phased-array antennas that electronically steer narrow beams toward rapidly orbiting AakashNet satellites via the Ku/Ka band. These satellites communicate not only with ground stations but also with each other through laser-based inter-satellite links, creating a resilient, low-latency communication mesh in space. Ground gateways connected to ISRO’s ISTRAC manage satellite telemetry, internet routing, and network optimization.

Benefits:

  • Universal Access: Extends broadband to remote regions where fiber is impractical.
  • National Security: Provides fully encrypted, sovereign communication lines for defense and governance.
  • Economic Efficiency: Indigenous mass manufacturing and reusable launch systems drastically lower per-satellite and terminal costs.
  • Operational Flexibility: Mobile connectivity for aviation, maritime, and defense mobility.
  • Scalable Infrastructure: A modular system that can expand coverage and capacity as needed.

Intended Impact:
AakashNet bridges India’s digital divide by connecting 700+ million offline citizens, strengthening national defense autonomy, and empowering sectors like education, healthcare, and e-governance. It supports the Digital India and Atmanirbhar Bharat missions by ensuring that India’s communication backbone is built, managed, and secured within its borders.

Development Tools and Technology Stack:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS (Tailwind), JavaScript
  • Hosting: Locally hosted interface (no backend), simulating user dashboard and satellite control visualization.
  • Hardware Simulation: Modeled phased-array terminal design and link budgeting through MATLAB and OpenEMS (for RF performance).
  • Software Logic: Prototype control and visualization scripts written in JavaScript for demonstrating network topology, beam switching, and data throughput visualization.
  • Design Assets: 2D/3D mockups of terminal hardware and coverage dashboard for real-time user interaction.

Creativity and Innovation:
The project reimagines satellite internet as a sovereign national infrastructure rather than a private service. Its phased-array antenna approach eliminates mechanical tracking, enabling compact, low-maintenance terminals. The use of a laser-linked mesh among satellites reduces ground dependency and enhances latency performance. On the software side, the frontend dashboard was built using lightweight web technologies (HTML, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript) to visualize live satellite coverage, beam steering, and bandwidth analytics — without requiring a backend, making it simple and portable.

Design Considerations:

  • Affordability: Designed for mass production with hardware cost capped at ₹23,000 per terminal.
  • Sovereignty: Full Indian control over design, manufacturing, and launch (via ISRO–HAL–BHEL collaboration).
  • Reliability: Resilient network with multiple failover paths through inter-satellite communication.
  • Security: AES-256 and WPA3 standards with a roadmap toward Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC).
  • Scalability: Architecture supports commercial, rural, and defense-grade variants with tailored service plans.

In essence, AakashNet is more than just a satellite internet solution, it’s a step toward India’s digital self-reliance, enabling universal, secure, and sovereign connectivity across every corner of the nation.

projectDetails.name: PureFlow
projectDetails.summary:
We developed PureFlow, an interactive systems engineering platform that allows users to design, model in 3D, and validate space habitats. It directly addresses the challenge by enabling the creation of layouts and volumes, but it goes further: the system calculates critical crew requirements in real-time (mass, power, life support) based on crew size and mission duration, providing instant feedback on the design's viability.

Its importance lies in being more than a layout tool; it is a survival simulator. With its unique integration of NASA's DONKI API, PureFlow tests the design against real space weather threats, such as solar storms. It doesn't just answer if a habitat can be built, but if its crew can survive in it, making resilient design a fundamental priority.
projectDetails.details:
PureFlow: Would Your Habitat Survive a Solar Storm... Today?
We are standing on the brink of interplanetary civilization. But between our dreams of Martian colonies and lunar bases lies a brutal reality: space is unforgiving. It’s not enough to build a shelter; we must engineer a self sustaining ecosystem. PureFlow is more than a design tool. It's the crucible where your deep space habitat is tested against the harsh, unpredictable truths of the cosmos.

What is PureFlow?
PureFlow is your command center for mission architecture. This interactive platform empowers you to design, simulate, and validate a complete space habitat for any destination, such as the Moon, Mars, or deep space. Step into the role of Mission Architect. From the initial briefing to the final 3D model, PureFlow is your dedicated systems engineer, instantly analyzing the ripple effects of every choice you make.

Features That Define the Future:
From Blueprint to Reality in 3D
Forget static blueprints. With PureFlow, you sculpt your habitat in a dynamic 3D environment. Place crew quarters, connect life support, and position science labs. With every click, our physics engine provides immediate feedback, calculating critical shifts in mass, power draw, and internal volume. You don't just design a habitat; you watch it come alive.

The Logistics of Life
A crew of four on Mars needs tons of supplies. Or do they? PureFlow runs a deep survival simulation, modeling the entire life support loop. Integrate advanced ECLSS or a greenhouse, and see the numbers change in real time. Witness exactly how recycling and in situ resources can slash your launch mass, turning an impossible mission into a feasible one.

Armor Against the Elements
A Martian dust storm can shred exposed materials. Lunar radiation is relentless. Your habitat's skin is its first and last line of defense. Choose your armor, from advanced titanium composites to 3D printed native regolith. PureFlow’s analysis engine immediately pits your choice against the specific environmental hazards of your destination, revealing vulnerabilities before they become fatal.

The Decisive Difference: A Live Link to the Sun
This is what truly sets PureFlow apart. We are plugged directly into NASA's DONKI, the Space Weather Database. This isn't a historical model. It's live. When a solar flare erupts from the sun right now, an alert flashes across your screen. Your habitat is hit with the full force of the storm in your simulation. Is the shielding enough? Is the storm shelter positioned correctly? PureFlow doesn't just prepare you for a theoretical threat. It tests your creation against the cosmos as it is, today.

Our Mission: Engineering for Resilience
The next giant leap depends on tools that are as tough, smart, and adaptable as our astronauts. PureFlow was born from this conviction. We fuse immersive 3D design with rigorous systems engineering and live, unpredictable data from space itself. We exist to answer the only question that matters: Is your crew's new home ready?

Because in the void, survival is just the starting point. We're designing for life.

projectDetails.name: Astro Sweepers – AI‑powered orbital debris compliance and risk intelligence
projectDetails.summary: Astro Sweepers is a compliance‑and‑insight platform that automates NASA’s Debris Assessment Software (DAS) workflow, generates ODAR/EOMP reports and produces clear, actionable risk scores for space operators. It uses our proprietary ASRI index to weight debris legacy, compliance readiness, collision‑risk burden and sustainability alignment, combining NASA SPARK/Space‑Track data and DAS outputs to produce before and after risk scores and long‑term debris population forecasts. The system includes a user‑friendly web portal that transforms technical analyses into intuitive dashboards and business‑ready reports, helping customers reduce post‑mission lifetimes, lower casualty risks and demonstrate regulatory compliance to insurers, investors and agencies. Ultimately, Astro Sweepers aims to mitigate the mounting orbital‑debris crisis by tying immediate DAS compliance with longer‑term sustainability forecasting and a scalable business model, enabling safer, more sustainable access to low Earth orbit.
projectDetails.details:
1. Detailed Project Description

What Astro Sweepers Does

Astro Sweepers is an end‑to‑end orbital debris compliance and risk‑intelligence platform. It automatically ingests public orbital data (from NASA SPARK 2022, Space‑Track TLEs/CDMs and ESA DISCOS), generates Debris Assessment Software (DAS) reports (DAS, ODAR, EOMP) and computes the Astro Sweepers Risk Index (ASRI) for every resident space object. Operators can upload a satellite’s two‑line element (TLE) or choose from our database and receive a real‑time assessment of their mission’s compliance status and collision risk, along with mitigation recommendations, dashboards and downloadable PDF reports.

How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

  1. DCRA v3 Risk Scoring: We devised a physics‑based formula to approximate each object’s collision risk before running DAS. The DCRA_BASE combines four weighted components:
    • D (Debris Legacy) – age and object type (rocket body, debris, payload).
    • C (Compliance) – proxies for meeting end‑of‑life rules: perigee altitude, age and debris flag.
    • R (Risk Burden) – a 2‑D Gaussian‑smoothed altitude–inclination density map, eccentricity (apo‑peri spread) and radar cross‑section (size).
    • S (Sustainability Alignment) – perigee feasibility and eccentricity.
      We further normalized the Δv required to deorbit (via vis‑viva) and blended it into C and S. The macro weights (R=0.45, D=0.25, C=0.20, S=0.10) emerged from sensitivity studies using the SPARK data.
    • (below image generated by chat gpt)
  2. Δv‑Integrated Compliance Model: For each object we computed the single‑burn Δv to lower perigee to a target (120 km or 550 km). DAS runs then determined the new post‑mission lifetime, casualty expectation and disposal compliance. Our DCRA_WITH_DAS = DCRA_BASE × (1 − DAS_REDUCTION), where DAS_REDUCTION (0 – 0.5) credits young payloads, low‑perigee disposal and controlled reentries. This elegantly marries the qualitative risk index with quantitative compliance gains.
  3. Selection Algorithms: To identify problematic objects fairly across nations, we used DCRA_BASE ranking and Pc from Conjunction Data Messages (CDMs). First we selected the Top 50 objects by DCRA across all countries. Then to ensure equitable representation, we selected Top 3 per country (U.S., Russia, China, India, ESA/EU and “Others”) for the Top 15 case studies. Each object’s risk components and potential Δv were tabulated; this fairness prevents bias toward countries with the largest constellations.
  4. Auto‑Generation of ODAR/EOMP: Our scripts populated NASA’s ODAR/EOMP templates using OMM data, TLE‑derived orbits and Δv plans. Operators receive a ready‑to‑submit compliance package, saving weeks of manual paperwork.

Business Model Integration:

The platform’s revenue model has eight tiers (ASRI Lite, Compliance Pack, Pro, Monitor, Operator License, Insurer License, Onboarding, University Research). This creates recurring SaaS income while offering regulatory and insurance synergies. Our audited financial model (2025–2028) shows break‑even after ~60 missions, 80 % gross margin on software, and expansion into debris removal/recycling in later phases.

Benefits and Goals

Astro Sweepers delivers immediate value by reducing mission analysis time, improving regulatory compliance and lowering insurance premiums. The ASRI dashboard empowers operators to see their risk in the context of the entire population and take proactive action. Over the long term, our system aims to flatten the growth curve of orbital debris, turn waste into an economic resource through in‑orbit recycling and help insurers and governments set fairer premiums and policies. The platform serves as a stepping stone toward active debris removal and material harvesting (Phase 2 of business roadmap).

Presenting DAS & ASRI Results

Representative Satellite Case Study – China‐1 CZ‑2C R/B

  • Baseline (No DAS): The object orbits at 613×671 km, 98.4° inclination and is >11 years old. Its DCRA components were high (R≈0.75, D≈0.93, C≈0.81, S≈0.58), yielding DCRA_BASE ≈ 0.79. DAS predicted a post‑mission lifetime >100 years and Ec≈3.3×10⁻⁴ (1:3,000) with a large casualty area (~30 m²). It failed requirements 4.6–4.7.
  • Drop‑to‑550 km (Δv ≈ 22 m/s): A single apogee burn lowered perigee to 550 km. Post‑mission lifetime dropped below 25 years, Ec fell to 4.1×10⁻⁵ (1:28,500) and casualty area to 3.19 m². DAS compliance status changed to “Compliant” across 4.3–4.7, and DCRA_WITH_DAS = 0.60 (25 % improvement).
  • Robustness: Varying the area‑to‑mass ratio between 0.03–0.05 m²/kg, the perigee 525–575 km, or switching materials (Al 2024, steel, Ti) all still satisfied the 25‑year rule and casualty criteria. A controlled‑reentry test (perigee 120 km, Δv ≈ 142 m/s) produced Ec < 1×10⁻⁴, offering a second disposal option.
  • Also want to point out, We began with a CZ-2C rocket body at 613×671 km, 98.4°, over 11 years old—DAS gave >100 years lifetime and Ec ≈ 3.3×10⁻⁴, so it failed. We toggled PMD in DAS and set a single apogee burn to lower perigee to 550 km (Δv ≈ 22 m/s). Re-running DAS dropped lifetime below 25 years, casualty area to 3.19 m², and Ec to 4.1×10⁻⁵—now compliant across 4.3–4.7. We stress-tested A/M, materials, and perigee bands; all remained compliant. Our tool then auto-generated the ODAR/EOMP with the new orbit and disposal plan. A small, targeted burn—fully documented and audit-ready—turned risk into compliance.

  • ODAR/EOMP & Compliance Story: The platform auto‑filled the ODAR sections (launch vehicle, mission duration, disposal plan) and EOMP (deorbit burn details, passivation measures) based on the new orbit. This demonstrates our system’s ability to produce NASA‑ready compliance documentation.
  1. Classification & Decay Probability: trained a CNN on a Kaggle dataset of orbiting objects (derived from NASA imagery) to distinguish between debris, rocket bodies and payloads, estimating time‑to‑re‑entry. This work is exploratory; it has not yet been integrated into the Space Apps submission but may inform future ASRI weight calibrations.
  2. Adaptive Weighting: In future, our model could analyzelarge historical datasets to refine the macro weights (D, C, R, S) in DCRA v3; for now, the weights come from sensitivity studies using the SPARK‑2022 dataset and DAS results.
  3. Anomaly Detection: By training on CDMs, the model flags objects whose collision probability (Pc) is rising unusually fast. This functionality is a proposed feature for later phases of the Astro Sweepers platform.

ASRI‑Integrated Long‑Term Forecast

  • Population Simulation: Using the DAS population evolution module (2025–2100), three scenarios were modelled:
    1. Without DAS: ~21,800 objects >10 cm by 2100, mean Pc ≈ 3.8×10⁻⁴, mean lifetime ≈ 95 years, controlled reentry 14 %, ASRI ≈ 0.82.
    2. With DAS (2025 only): ~18,400 objects, Pc ≈ 2.4×10⁻⁴, lifetime ≈ 42 years, controlled reentry 48 %, ASRI ≈ 0.53.
    3. With DAS + ASRI (2100): ~11,200 objects, Pc ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁴, lifetime ≈ 23 years, controlled reentry 82 %, ASRI ≈ 0.32.
  • Interpretation: Implementing DAS compliance alone cuts collision risk by ~37 %, whereas adding ASRI Prioritization drives a ~70 % reduction in Pc, ~50 % fewer objects and ~75 % shorter residual lifetimes. This underscores the systemic impact of coupling compliance enforcement with intelligent risk Prioritization.
  • Visualization: Prepare two line charts – one for object count vs. time and another for mean Pc vs. time – showing the three trajectories. Also include a bar chart for ASRI (0.82 vs. 0.53 vs. 0.32).

Strategic Roadmap for Future ML Expansion

While the Space Apps submission is DAS‑centric, we have sketched a credible ML roadmap that extends our platform’s value:

not to forget we already have one machine learning model deployed and Astro sweepers is further planning to launch and train many more.

  1. Physics‑Informed Models: Develop neural networks that learn orbital dynamics and drag under varying solar cycles—leading to better lifetime predictions.
  2. Conjunction Prediction GNNs: Use graph neural networks on conjunction data to anticipate multi‑body interactions and cascade risks.
  3. Material & Mass Classification: Apply computer vision on radar or optical data to identify material composition for salvage, recycling and casualty modelling.
  4. Insurance & Pricing AI: Use ASRI scores and mission parameters to predict claim likelihoods and set dynamic premiums (link to your “Insurer License” tier).
  5. Debris Removal Robotics: Leverage reinforcement learning to control small sweepers for capture and deorbit missions. This ties into your Phase 2 hardware plans.

Recommendations & Vision – Science‑Driven Solutions

how our platform addresses both immediate compliance and long‑term sustainability:

  • Universal DAS Compliance: Advocate mandatory ODAR/EOMP submission for every LEO mission. Your platform automates this process, lowering the barrier for small operators and ensuring standardization.
  • Continuous ASRI Monitoring: Offer a publicly accessible dashboard that updates weekly, helping regulators and operators see real‑time risk changes and encouraging early mitigation.
  • Active Debris Removal & Recycling: Outline your Phase 2 vision—deploying small sweepers to deorbit derelict objects and harvest usable materials. Stress that this is a business opportunity and a sustainability imperative.
  • Low‑Δv Mission Design: Use your Δv‑integrated model to advise designers on optimal perigee altitudes (e.g. ~550 km) that achieve <25‑year re‑entry with minimal fuel.
  • Open Data Sharing: Call for an international data‑sharing framework (perhaps under UNOOSA) so that all nations can contribute TLE, CDM and material data, improving ML models and risk assessments.

LEO Accords & UN Angle

The LEO Accords concept acts as our policy proposal that meshes with UN Sustainable Development Goals. Include these elements:

  • DAS & ODAR/EOMP Requirement: All signatories must adhere to NASA‑STD 8719.14spaceappschallenge.org and file disposal plans. Your platform can provide the technical infrastructure.
  • Salvage & Recycling Rights: Define legal frameworks for debris removal and profit‑sharing from recycled materials.
  • Equity Measures: Provide discounted compliance services and training to emerging space nations; tie this to the “University Research” and “Lite” tiers.
  • UN Clearinghouse: Propose a UN‑hosted database for ASRI scores and compliance statuses, promoting transparency and accountability.
  • Alignment with SDGs: Highlight the link to SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) and SDG 13 (Climate Action)spaceappschallenge.org, reinforcing that orbital sustainability is part of global sustainable development.

Business Model, Profitability & Sustainability

Integrate our financial statement, revenue model and executive summary :

  • SaaS Core: Subscription tiers (Lite, Compliance Pack, Pro, Monitor) generate recurring revenue with 80 % gross margins. For example, small operators pay $300–$1,200 per month, while large constellations subscribe at $50k–$150k per year; these tiers correspond to DCRA scoring, compliance automation and continuous monitoring.
  • Licensing & Partnerships: The Operator License allows large operators to integrate ASRI directly into their planning pipelines; the Insurer License offers risk scores and compliance verification to insurers, enabling risk‑based premium pricing.
  • Onboarding & Research: One‑time fees and discounted academic access promote early adoption and knowledge sharing, supporting capacity building.
  • Long‑Term Expansion: High‑margin software revenues fund future hardware (sweeper drones) and recycling initiatives, capturing new revenue streams from recovered materials.
  • Financial Transparency: Refer to your audited IFRS statements (2025–2028) and the detailed revenue model—these show break‑even within ~60 missions and growth to $500M+ ARR by the end of the decade. This demonstrates both economic viability and sustainability, which judges value.

Stress that profitability and environmental stewardship are mutually reinforcing: a clean, safe LEO environment ensures commercial viability, and your business model incentivizes compliance and debris removal.

projectDetails.name: Queñaris
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Queñaris, a platform for the smart reforestation of queñua forests. It is a comprehensive system that combines the use of native microorganisms, NASA satellite data, drones, and artificial intelligence to accelerate tree growth, identify the best areas for reforestation, and monitor the health of the ecosystem.
The project addresses critical water scarcity in Arequipa, caused by the degradation of queñua forests, which are vital for water retention. While traditional reforestation methods are slow and not very scalable, our platform uses technology to create a massive and efficient strategy. By digitizing the terrain and analyzing phenological data, we can make evidence-based decisions to maximize the impact of each tree planted.
This is crucial because the loss of queñua forests has a direct impact on water security in Arequipa. The drastic reduction in spring flow (from 14 L/s to 0 in days) threatens the water supply for human consumption, agribusiness (28.5%), energy (67.7%), and mining (11%), creating the risk of food crises and social conflicts. Restoring these forests means restoring the water balance and ensuring a sustainable future for the region.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do? 

Queñaris is a decision support system for large-scale reforestation. Specifically:

  • It digitizes and analyzes high Andean ecosystems using drones and satellite data.
  • It identifies optimal areas for reforestation based on plant health indicators, soil moisture, and other key variables.
  • It accelerates the growth and survival rate of queñua seedlings (to 25 cm/year and >80% survival) through the use of native microorganisms.
  • It monitors the phenology and health of reforested forests over time to ensure their sustainability.
  • Centralizes all information on a web platform so that communities and organizations can plan and execute massive reforestation campaigns.

How does it work?

The process follows a structured workflow:

  1. Geospatial Digitization: Drone flights are conducted to capture high-resolution images and georeference the area of interest, creating a detailed orthomosaic.
  2. Satellite Data Analysis: Data from NASA's LP DAAC is used to calculate vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI, NDMI, etc.) that measure the health, greenness, and moisture content of existing vegetation.
  3. AI Integration and Modeling: Drone and satellite data are integrated. An artificial intelligence model analyzes this combined information to identify the best areas and conditions for planting.
  4. Biological Preparation: In nurseries, the 5,000 queñua seedlings are strengthened with native microorganisms (mycorrhizae, Trichoderma) to double their growth rate and resistance.
  5. Execution and Monitoring: Massive reforestation campaigns are carried out in the identified areas. The platform continues to monitor progress in the short, medium, and long term.

What benefits does it have?

Environmental: Restores a key ecosystem, combats desertification, increases water retention (each tree can retain up to 20 liters per day), and promotes water recharge in springs and wetlands.

Social: Ensures a constant water supply for hundreds of local families and communities, reducing the risk of social conflicts due to water scarcity.

Economic: Increases the efficiency and success of reforestation projects, protecting water-dependent industries such as agriculture, energy, and mining. Our business model is based on offering processing and monitoring services per hectare, ensuring the sustainability of the project.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to carry out a first large-scale reforestation project in December with the 5,000 seedlings we already have ready, validating our model in the field. In the long term, we seek to reverse the degradation of the 100,000 hectares of queñua forests that historically existed, ensuring water security in the Arequipa region and creating a smart reforestation model that can be replicated in other Andean ecosystems.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, Node.js, npm/yarn, Docker, Loveable( initial template)
  • Infrastructure and Technological Hosting: Vercel (Frontend), Google AI Studio (Gemini API), GitHub Pages, GitHub Cloud, Cloudinary (Image Storage)
  • Backend & API: Django 5.0.6, Django REST Framework, PostgreSQL with GeoDjango, Redis, Celery, Gunicorn
  • Frontend & UI: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5, CSS3, TailwindCSS, Shadcn/UI, Radix UI Components
  • Programming Languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL
  • AI & Machine Learning: Google Gemini Pro API 2.5, Geospatial Analysis, Rasterio, GeoPandas
  • Data Processing & Geospatial: Pillow, Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, GDAL, Fiona, EarthAccess (NASA/USGS), Metashape Agisoft, QGIS
  • Async Tasks & Caching: Celery, Redis, Django Channels, Django Celery Beat
  • Software & Design: QGIS (geospatial processing), Google Colab (AI prototyping), Adobe Premier
  • Hardware: DJI Matrice 4 Series Drone, Development and analysis computers
  • Data Sources: Satellite imagery (NASA/USGS), Aerial drone georeferenced orthomosaic, GPS metadata, HDF5 datasets

Plus:(Workflows, Drone-Contoller and Seedlings for reforestation)

projectDetails.name: Project Gaia+LEO
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Gaia-LEO, a mixed-integer optimization framework that co-designs orbital and terrestrial data-center networks for the next generation of AI and Earth-observation workloads. The model jointly optimizes facility location, network topology, and workload placement by minimizing total CapEx + OpEx while satisfying real-world physical constraints latency, bandwidth, power, and thermal limits. Each orbital module represents a 40 MW containerized data-center node with solar power and radiative cooling; ground sites anchor fiber backhaul and user access. Using inputs from NASA’s CO2 emissions, water & orbital debris data and web scraped data center data the solver decides which orbital clusters to launch, which ground points of presence to activate, and how to route traffic through optical & inter-satellite links.

This framework directly addresses the challenge of commercializing LEO by quantifying when and where orbital compute becomes economically advantageous compared with terrestrial infrastructure. It transforms space from a communications relay into a computational layer – a sustainable, solar-powered extension of Earth’s cloud. The result is an actionable blueprint for scaling AI training and climate modeling in orbit, reducing terrestrial power and water footprints, and accelerating humanity’s transition toward space-based green compute as part of the emerging orbital economy.
projectDetails.details:
Re-thinking where the Earth's compute should live.

Gaia-LEO is a data-driven simulation and optimization framework that designs hybrid orbital–terrestrial data center networks for sustainable AI and Earth-observation compute. Built with Python, Three.JS, and Streamlit, the system implements a mixed-integer optimization (MIP) that decides where to build orbital and Earth-based data centers, what optimal balances are required between both compute options, and how to route workloads to minimize total cost (CapEx + OpEx) under physical constraints on latency, bandwidth, power, and thermal limits.

The model integrates NASA POWER data, US energy-grid data, and available public data on terrestrial data centers and costs to simulate real-world environmental and economic trade-offs. Each orbital module represents a 40 MW solar-powered, radiatively-cooled compute node, while ground sites are built for resilience, redundancy, and inference.

The Streamlit interface allows users to interactively explore scenarios, visualize cost-performance trade-offs, and identify when orbital compute becomes environmentally advantageous and profitable. The project’s creativity lies in merging operations-research optimization with environmental modeling and space-systems engineering. 

The development of new data centers is not going to slow down any time soon. We need a more sustainable option to invest in technological advancements while also designing for the future in a scalable and environmentally-friendly way. Gaia-LEO can inform policymakers, governments, and cloud providers on when, where, and how to scale sustainable orbital compute, reducing terrestrial energy and water footprints while enabling a greener and more resilient orbital economy.

projectDetails.name: SkySense
projectDetails.summary:
SkySense is a web-app platform that uses NASA Earth observation data and AI analysis to provide ultra-local and personalized weather predictions. Our goal is to help users plan outdoor events, sports, and travel with greater accuracy and confidence. By integrating NASA, Google, and Gemini APIs, SkySense analyzes multiple weather variables such as rain, wind, temperature, humidity, and visibility to generate real-time risk assessments and suggest the safest time windows for activities. 
The platform also features TwisterBot, a smart conversational assistant that delivers adaptive alerts, reminders, and weather insights directly to the user.
SkySense addresses the challenge of unreliable, generic forecasts by making meteorological data understandable and actionable. It would empower individuals and organizations to make informed decisions, reduce weather-related risks, and transform uncertainty into confidence.
projectDetails.details: SkySense was developed using React.js for a dynamic and responsive front-end experience, supported by Firebase for user authentication, cloud storage, and hosting. It integrates Google APIs to handle calendar synchronization, notifications, and secure Google sign-ins. For environmental intelligence, it connects to NASA’s POWER Data Access Viewer, NASA POWER API, and Open-Meteo datasets, which provide real-time data on temperature, humidity, wind speed, radiation, and precipitation. The predictive model processes this information to generate comfort-based insights, while the Gemini API powers the conversational assistant, enabling natural interaction with users. The design was created in Figma, ensuring a glassy, minimal, and accessible interface across all devices. Together, these technologies make SkySense a seamless bridge between AI, design, and space-based data.

projectDetails.name: Henry's Farm Adventures
projectDetails.summary:
Welcome to Henry’s Farm Adventure!
For the NASA Farm Navigators Challenge, we didn’t just build a game, we built a global farming quest powered by space data.

Meet Henry, a struggling farmer whose crops keep failing. Instead of giving up, he sets off on an epic journey around the world, guided by real NASA satellite data. Along the way, he meets farmers on the frontlines of climate change, like Bilal in Pakistan, fighting the floods of 2022, and Ramesh in India, surviving brutal heatwaves.

But this isn’t just a story, it’s you in action. As the player, you step into Henry’s boots and take on mini-games that transform serious challenges into hands-on missions, by solving them, you learn how farmers adapt in real life, how NASA’s data reveals these risks, and how communities can fight back against climate change.

This is NASA data like you’ve never seen it before, not in charts or reports, but in the palm of your hand, as a playful, high-stakes adventure.
projectDetails.details:
Zumorroda-X's Project Solution

Henry’s Farm Adventure is an educational adventure game designed to teach players how environmental challenges affect agriculture turning real NASA satellite data into an interactive story-driven game. Players travel with Henry, meet farmers worldwide, and use hands-on mini games to solve climate challenges making science both fun and accessible.

How Does Our Solution Work

In the game, Henry is a farmer facing repeated crop failures, and he sets out on a journey to uncover the environmental challenges threatening agriculture as floods, heatwaves, droughts, and soil salinization. Along the way, Henry meets farmers from different countries who share their experiences and solutions, helping him piece together which challenge might also be affecting his own farm.

  • Heatwaves (India, 2021):
    Henry visits Ramesh, a farmer in India, who experienced the devastating 2021 extreme heat crisis. Ramesh shows Henry NASA's extreme heat map, in which player can see India suffering badly from heat in addition to other areas, then teaches Henry about techniques farmers use to protect crops from heats such as shade nets and mulching, after that Ramesh tests player with a quiz game.
  • Floods (Pakistan, 2022):
    In Pakistan, Henry meets Bilal, who describes how the historic 2022 floods devastated farmland. Using an image slider, Henry compares NASA satellite images of Pakistan before and after the flood, witnessing the disaster’s true scale. In the gameplay, players help Henry protect farms:
      Level 1: Navigate Henry to place straw in the areas hit by the heaviest rainfall.
      Level 2: Install drainage pipes to save waterlogged fields. Through this, players learn how farmers can adapt and reduce flood damage.
  • Soil Salinization (Egypt 2021):
    Next, Henry travels to Egypt to meet Mohamed, who shows him how irrigation practices are affecting farmland. Henry learns about soil salinization and explores live NASA satellite data that reveals how salt buildup reduces soil productivity over time. In the gameplay, players are given a time limit to save the farm from salinization by:
      Task: Implementing drip irrigation to revive the salty plants.
    Through this, players discover how efficient irrigation methods can protect soil health.
  • Drought (United States):
    Henry also visits the United States, where he meets an American farmer "Sam" struggling with drought. He learns how drought affects soil health and how scientists use vegetation indexes from satellite imagery to measure water stress and monitor crops.
  • Crops Management (Brazil):
    Finally, Henry visits João da Silva, a farmer and innovator. João explains how increasing CO₂ levels can sometimes stimulate plant growth. He also emphasizes the importance of adaptation to climate change, using fertilizers wisely, adjusting planting times, and adopting new techniques. João then reveals his AI model, which predicts which crops will survive based on country, year, CO₂ levels, and adaptation strategies. To make it hands-on, he shows Henry a NASA food supply table and turns it into a matching game, where Henry pairs crops with the right conditions, learning how to choose the best crops for each scenario.

When the player completes all the challenges, the farmers gather together for a lively catch-up!

The game benefits

farmers, students, and the wider community by:

  • Educating players on environmental disasters and their impact on crops.
  • Demonstrating practical, data-driven strategies for sustainable farming.
  • Bridging the gap between NASA’s datasets and real-world agricultural practices in a fun, engaging way.

Our goal

To make NASA’s open data more accessible, helping communities prepare for climate-related agricultural challenges while fostering awareness of global environmental issues. Despite our attempt to reveal agricultural difficulties globally, our game is limited to certain issues and didn't mention other calamities faced by other countries such as wildfires.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • Python → for the ML model.
  • JavaScript (with Phaser) → for 2D game development.

Data Sources:

  • NASA real-time datasets → for environmental and agricultural data. Through NASA’s data, we were able to access Landsat images that allowed us to compare countries' farmlands before and after enduring environmental issues, that go back to a farmland in 1984 and compare it with the same area about 17 years later. Furthermore, NASA provides data that allows us to check recent NDVI (Natural differentiation vegetation index) of different countries, which was integrated in our games using APIs. In addition, an artificial intelligence model was used and integrated with the NASA data to highlight the significance of CO2 on crops, and adaptation level on different types of crops. Finally, data was extracted from NASA’s US drought monitor, displayed in a map, and utilized for learning purposes in the game.

Character Design:

  • Piskel → for creating and editing pixel-style images and sprites.

projectDetails.name: Project Resonant Exoplanets
projectDetails.summary:
Resonant Worlds Explorer is an AI-powered system that ingests telescope and satellite data, including spectra from missions like JWST, to search for exoplanets and detect possible biosignatures. Unlike traditional tools that rely on approximate floating-point methods, our system integrates Modulus, a new exact-math solver that converts physics and chemistry problems into number theory and solves them without numerical error. This allows us to model planetary atmospheres with high precision, test chemical equilibrium, and distinguish true biosignatures (like O₂ + CH₄ coexistence) from abiotic false positives.
We built a full end-to-end pipeline: fetching NASA data, detecting exoplanets with transit algorithms, validating signals with physics models, and running Modulus-based chemistry checks. Results are presented in a web interface with visual plots and automatically generated scientific reports.
This matters because the search for life beyond Earth depends on accuracy. By combining astronomy data, physics validation, and exact chemistry, Resonant Worlds Explorer reduces false positives and provides a reliable way to identify promising candidates for habitability, helping guide future missions and discoveries.
projectDetails.details:
Resonant Worlds Explorer is a full-stack application that combines astronomy data, machine learning, and exact physics to detect exoplanets and identify potential biosignatures. The system ingests data from NASA missions such as Kepler, TESS, and JWST, preprocesses light curves or spectra, and runs transit detection algorithms to find planets. Once candidates are found, it validates them with physics models and uses Modulus, our exact-math solver, to analyze atmospheric chemistry. This allows us to check whether molecules like O₂, CH₄, and O₃ can coexist naturally or require biological replenishment.

The benefits are accuracy and reliability: traditional AI can misclassify or hallucinate results, but our solver eliminates numerical error and dramatically reduces false positives. The intended impact is to provide scientists with a trustworthy, scalable tool for finding habitable worlds and prioritizing targets for future exploration.

We built the project with Python (FastAPI, XGBoost, Lightkurve, Astroquery), TypeScript/React, and Google Cloud integration. Modulus is based on a modified Qwen transformer that we extended into the Prime Algebra Transformer, enabling exact arithmetic for physics and chemistry problems.

The project is creative because it blends machine learning with hard physics, turning exoplanet discovery into an interactive, explainable, and reproducible process. We considered both scientific rigor and usability, delivering not just code but also visual plots, automated PDF reports, and a clear workflow that makes complex science accessible.

projectDetails.name: SpaceGenes+: A Synergy Dashboard for Molecular Space Health
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceGenes+ is an interactive dashboard designed to uncover synergistic gene expression changes in space biology: specifically, how radiation and microgravity together impact astronaut health at the molecular level. Using real NASA GeneLab datasets (OSD-288 Transcriptome analysis of murine spleen in space), our tool identifies genes like TP53, ATM, and GADD45A that exhibit non-additive responses when exposed to multiple spaceflight stressors.

This dashboard empowers researchers, drug developers, and mission planners to quickly visualize synergy effects across different conditions: radiation only, microgravity only, and combined spaceflight. In future, users will be able to filter by organ system, biological function, and stressor type, enabling faster hypothesis generation and precision targeting for space medicine and cancer biology.

SpaceGenes+ addresses a major challenge: most space omics tools treat stressors in isolation. Yet, in real missions, astronauts experience overlapping biological stress. Recognizing these hidden molecular interactions is essential for developing protective measures and advancing long-duration spaceflight.
projectDetails.details:
SpaceGenes+ is a web-based interactive dashboard designed to reveal synergistic gene expression changes in response to combined spaceflight stressors—namely radiation and microgravity. Traditionally, biological data from space studies examine these stressors in isolation. Our platform uniquely surfaces how they interact to amplify cellular risks like DNA damage, immune suppression, and cancer susceptibility.

How it works:
SpaceGenes+ ingests transcriptomic datasets (currently featuring NASA GeneLab OSD-288) and calculates synergy scores based on fold-change in gene expression across conditions. It detects when gene activation under combined stress exceeds the sum of individual effects—flagging key "synergy genes" using an automated formula.

Key Benefits & Impact:

  • Helps space biologists prioritize genes for further study.
  • Aids drug developers in finding therapeutic targets.
  • Supports NASA planners in understanding organ-level risks for long-duration missions.
  • Offers visual, non-code-based access to large genomics datasets.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Framer: front-end website and animation
  • Bolt: dashboard and data visualization engine
  • Python (Pandas, NumPy): for preprocessing and synergy calculations
  • Figma/FigJam: design and prototyping
  • Google Sheets/CSV: data curation

Creative Elements:

  • Built to be researcher-friendly with exportable visuals,
  • Includes a compelling story that connects molecular insights to real astronaut risks,
  • Uses an interface that simplifies complex bioinformatics into visual exploration.
